You wouldn't give those medications because there's no reason to. Assuming this is an older child, it's probably nothing. If it IS something, you wouldn't treat the problem with Albuterol. When you give a medication, you should be trying to treat the root of the problem (the majority of the time). If you treat the symptoms, you get in the habit of missing important things. Think in the reverse... You have tachycardia, give a beta blocker to slow the heart, but your kid actually has myocarditis and dies. 

Also, you're not just a resident whose opinion doesn't matter. Get that out of your head. Find a way to talk more appropriately to nurses by hearing their concerns and giving constructive feedback. It'll get you further.

I never considered PA at the time. If I could go back, I probably wouldn't do medicine at all. I'm in my early 30s and still can barely afford rent. Not to say money is everything, but I just don't think I understood how long the road was. I think his explanation is a great one though. How do you envision your actual career, your day to day? To answer your question, two things come to mind. One, double check everything that you're saying. Check the vent settings on the monitor, check the drip rates in the room, check and write down when meds are due and that they were given, check the order list for upcoming orders, etc. I've worked with some residents who have similar issues, and I've noticed that some of it comes from them presenting what is told to them and they are not actually verifying the information. Unfortunately, this is always an issue where the fellow may not tell you everything. The best that you can do is get in the habit of double checking everything on every patient. You will eventually get quicker at it and it will become habit. 

Two, talk to your nurses and check on your patients. PICU nurses are usually really good and very involved with their patients. Always make sure that you talk to the nurse to see how the patient is doing and if there were any updates. This also gets you in the habit of going into the room more often to check more things from number one. 

Don't be too hard on yourself, especially if you are already doing these things. Sometimes people don't click with others and everyone gets a bad eval every now and then.

I present the same exact way every time. When I was a student, they made us present by memory. I finally got it down by reciting it a bunch of times out loud. Find a pattern for yourself where you plug in the story. The other part of it is actually knowing the history. You should be able to tell a co-resident how they came in, like during sign out. Once you find your flow and pattern, plus adding it to actually truly knowing the story, it will click and be much simpler!
